# Methods: metabolomics_untargeted

_Each sentence below is the decision record's own, as it stood when this bundle was exported: answers changed before anything was seen are folded out, every change made after the estimates were seen is kept and marked, and a sentence that counts rows counts them as they stand. Sections follow STROBE and STROBE-nut; a paragraph that is not the record's was written by the analysis on these answers._

## Study design (STROBE 4)

The analysis was declared for `inference`: associations are estimated with their uncertainty. Each row was declared a different participant: no one appears in more than one row.

## Participants (STROBE 6)

No rows were excluded: every row with `responder` measured stays in the analysis.

## Variables (STROBE 7)

`responder` was chosen as the outcome; it is measured on `72` of `80` rows. `1` of `responder` was taken as the event and coded 1; `0` was coded 0. Column roles were set for `399` columns: exposures `mz_0001`, `mz_0002`, `mz_0003` and 389 more; covariates `run_order`, `batch`, `age` and 2 more; identifier `sample_id`; excluded `sample_type`; `run_order`, `batch` and 392 more were proposed below high confidence and wait for their own confirmation before any default reads them. Confirmed together, each as the question showed it: `run_order` was confirmed as a covariate; `batch` was confirmed as a covariate; `392` columns (from `mz_0001`) were confirmed as an exposure. The analysis estimates the total effect of each exposure in turn on `responder`, as the difference in each exposure's mean between the event and the other level (the limma design), every member reported with its Benjamini–Hochberg q-value across all 392 tests. Confirmed together, each as the question showed it: `run_order` was confirmed to hold amounts or counts; `age` was confirmed to hold amounts or counts.

## Data sources and measurement (STROBE 8)

The table was read through the `metabolomics` lens. The table was confirmed as one row per sample, as supplied, and was not transposed. `8` rows where `sample_type` is `pooled_qc` (instrument runs, not participants) were excluded as reference rows before the held-out rows were drawn. Of the 394 intensity columns, those of them the models take as exposures were normalized by probabilistic quotient normalization (Dieterle et al. 2006), the reference spectrum the median of the integral-normalized training rows within each fold, then log2-transformed. `batch` enters the outcome model as a covariate, so batch differences are not read as biology (Nygaard, Rødland & Hovig 2016).

## Quantitative variables (STROBE 11)

`run_order` entered the models as a straight line; `age` entered the models as a straight line.

## Statistical methods (STROBE 12)

No rows were held out; performance was estimated by `5`-fold cross-validation (seed `0`, stratified by `responder`). For the effect of each exposure, by the disjunctive cause criterion: `age` and `sex` are confounders, adjusted for. For the effect of each exposure, by the disjunctive cause criterion: `bmi` is of unknown timing, left out of the primary model and adjusted for in a declared secondary one. For the effect of each exposure, by the disjunctive cause criterion: `run_order` and `batch` are causes of the exposure, adjusted for. One model family was chosen: feature-wise least-squares tests with Benjamini–Hochberg false-discovery control. Read from the values, no question asked: `sample_id` is the unit's identifier (Named like an identifier; it names rows or samples: `72` labels, one per row); `sample_type` is left out of the models (Every row holds the same value, so it cannot explain anything); `age` is a covariate (A person's characteristic, usually adjusted for rather than studied); `sex` is a covariate (A person's characteristic, usually adjusted for rather than studied); `bmi` is a covariate (A person's characteristic, usually adjusted for rather than studied); `responder` is a binary outcome (Only `0` and `1` — read as a binary outcome); `bmi` is an amount (one slope) (`65` values with decimals that fill their grid as a measurement's do (a code list's sit apart)); `sex` is coded F female, M male (the labels spell the sexes (`F` female)). Missing predictor values were imputed in each training fold without the outcome: the median for numbers, the most frequent value for categories; no row was dropped for a missing predictor; values below the detection limit in `mz_0022`, `mz_0121` and 304 more were set to their expected value below the limit under a censored-normal fit, in each training fold; it was kept under inference as a recorded limitation: a single fill treats each imputed value as measured, so the intervals are too narrow, and a median fill biases a coefficient whenever who is missing depends on another variable.

The estimate of each exposure is reported across a declared sequence of models fit on all 72 analyzed rows: unadjusted; Model 2, the primary, adjusted for `run_order`, `batch`, `age` and `sex`; Model 3, further adjusted for `bmi`, a possible mediator, so not a total effect. Only the exposure's estimates are shown as effects; every other coefficient is listed apart as an adjustment term, not an effect estimate (Westreich & Greenland 2013, Am J Epidemiol 177:292). 392 exposures were tested, each in turn; Benjamini–Hochberg q-values control the false-discovery rate across all 392 (Benjamini & Hochberg 1995, J R Stat Soc B 57:289), and every member is shown, significant or not.

Batch was included as a covariate. Intensities were normalized by probabilistic quotient normalization (Dieterle et al. 2006) and log2-transformed. Values below detection in 305 features were filled after normalization and before the log, each by its expected value below the limit under a left-censored normal fitted to the feature's logarithm on the analyzed rows (Lubin et al. 2004). A single fill, recorded as a limitation: its intervals are too narrow. Each of the 392 features was tested in its own linear model with the covariates; Benjamini–Hochberg q-values across the 392 tests (0 below 0.05), every feature shown.

The analysis plan recorded above was declared in TurboTab before any estimate was displayed (SHA-256 `92618492cf0c`); every later change is marked as made after the estimates were seen.

## Reproducibility

The analysis was run in TurboTab 2.0.0.dev0 (source revision `caa9563bbdfb`). The supplementary provenance record holds the decision log (`24` records), the SHA-256 of the input file `metabolomics_untargeted.csv` (SHA-256 `4b4954c3dd73`), the analysis plan (SHA-256 `92618492cf0c`) and the model matrix (`72` rows by `396` columns; SHA-256 `168d225a431b` as Parquet). Replaying it with `python -m turbotab.replay` checks each input file against its hash and refuses one that differs; otherwise it rebuilds the analysis from the input files and the decision log alone and compares the model matrix and every reported estimate with these.
